en: Oṃ. [Now begins the Vīraśaivācārapradīpikā.]
[The First Chapter]
Salutations to the glorious gurus.
Even for men who endure the suffering arising from many births, the Lord, with a gaze moistened by compassion, [acts].
I bow to him who, having beheld them, bestows his grace by granting them his own state. || 1 ||
Just as fragrance is in a flower, oil in sesame seeds, and luster in gold, so it is [in this].
I bow to the Goddess Śivā, who is inseparably connected through the relation of invariable concomitance. || 2 ||
Born from the ocean of Mādalāmbā’s womb, he is the jewel of the Vasu family.
I bow my head perpetually to the one whose nature is Dharma and who is the immovable pillar. || 3 ||
In the great village of Drākṣārāma, there was a teacher named Koṭipalla.
He was a knower of the truth of the Vedas and Vedānta, and a knower of the truth of the Purāṇas and Āgamas.
The kinsman who dispels the darkness of the flood of sins of his devoted worshippers who bow before him.
He remains ever intent upon promoting the conduct of Śiva. || 5 ||
He had a famous son named Bhīmapaṇḍita.
He had perfected his conduct in accordance with virtuous tradition and was an expert in the meaning of all the scriptures.
His wife was Gauramāmbā, endowed with all auspicious marks.
She who has cast away the veil of sins, the omniscient one of excellent complexion.
His son was the peaceful Mallikārjuna Paṇḍita.
With his mind intent on the worship of Śiva, he was the bestower of liberation upon his disciples. || 8 ||
He is the submarine fire for the ocean of Bhaṭṭa armies and the forest fire for the wilderness of Vedānta.
And Rāhu, the devourer of the moon, having assumed the form of a Cārvāka, grew exceedingly large.
In the exceedingly beautiful great abode of King Veṅgala Cola;
Having conquered all doctrines, he then repeatedly licks the threefold victory.
And his son, who was born, was indeed named Paṇḍitārādhya.
He who knows the true meaning of the root mantra is one who delights his beloved, Liberation.
And his son was Siddhāntavīrārādhya, a worshipper of Śiva.
He was a knower of all scriptures, possessed of great intelligence, and a sun that dispelled the darkness of his disciples' sins.
From his reflection was born the illustrious one, endowed with all excellent qualities.
The most excellent teacher, renowned as Guru Basaveśvara, [is he]. || 13 ||
He had two sons, Gaṅgādhara and Basavatīrthaka.
Their minds were presided over by Śiva, and they had reached the further shore of the meaning of all the scriptures.
At that time, two sons were born to that King Śrī Bhasava.
The noble Hiri and the noble Paṇḍita were endowed with virtues such as mastery over the sense objects. || 15 ||
That Paṇḍitārādhya-deva had an excellent son.
Pārvatī’s question to Śiva; the description of the origin of the *piṇḍa* as explained by Śiva;
[the disciple] named Guruliṅgadeva, who is intent upon the worship of Śiva. (16)
That illustrious lord of teachers had excellent sons.
The first is Gurudeva, and the second is Paṇḍitārya. || 17 ||
The third is the one worshipped by Basava, and after that, the one worshipped by Jakkā.
Among them, the first was the renowned Gurudeva, who was exceedingly devoted.
He was requested by Siddhadeva, who was devoted to the worship of Śiva.
With a mind satisfied by the remaining faith born from the gravity of his conduct. || 19 ||
Having extracted the essence of all treatises, it is beneficial for the world beyond.
I shall compose this *Vīraśaivācārapradīpikā*, which bestows liberation.
(In the *Saṃsārapradīpikā*):
He is peaceful, pure by nature, and the embodiment of eternal bliss.
To the Lord, the bestower of boons, the sustainer of the universe, the husband of Umā; || 21 ||
The god of gods, the lord of the world, the yogi, the leader of those who bear the discus.
Having bowed her head to the Lord, the Goddess questioned him for the sake of liberation.
O Lord of the gods of gods, O Master, [cross] this ocean of saṃsāra which is difficult to traverse.
And tell me how animals cross over by means of an easy method. (23)
Śiva said:
Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate lady! You have asked a most auspicious question.
Now I shall fully explain this characteristic residing within the body.
That body of the self here which is produced by karma that is not mixed [with other factors].
Indeed, it should be understood as being of four kinds according to their respective dimensions. || 25 ||
Immovable beings, consisting of grasses, shrubs, and so forth, are to be known as *udbhijas* (those born from sprouting).
Worms, insects, moths, and the like are embodied beings known as those born from moisture.
Birds, snakes, crocodiles, fish, tortoises, and so forth are egg-born.
And humans and quadrupeds are to be known as those born from a womb (jarāyuja). || 27 ||
There, the ground, moistened by water and cooked by internal heat, [becomes fertile].
And being dispersed by the wind, it attains the state of a seed. || 28 ||
Whatever rice seeds are here again moistened with water.
They attain swelling, softness, and the state of being roots. || 29 ||
From that root arises the sprout, and from the sprout comes the production of leaves.
From the leaf comes the stalk, and from the stalk, in turn, the flower.
From the sprout comes the husked grain, and from the grain comes rice.
Then, from that rice, as well as from the cooked food and other medicinal herbs, [the following occurred]. || 31 ||
The seventeen [types of grain], beginning with barley and ending with śāli rice, are recorded as the best.
The medicinal herbs that end with the ripening of their fruit are proclaimed as the remaining minor ones. || 32 ||
They undergo transformation through the sixfold division of food.
Through the combination of their mutual flavors, they have attained manifold sweetness.
Eatable, chewable, drinkable, lickable, suckable, and slimy—thus is the description of the nature of the origin of the *piṇḍa*.
Furthermore, six varieties are declared, namely the six tastes beginning with sweet (*madhura*). (34)
And that food was consumed by embodied beings in large mouthfuls.
First, the vital breath (prāṇa) gradually establishes itself within the internal seat of the heart.
That wind divides the undivided food into two parts.
Having entered into the midst of the food, [he should offer] the food separately and the water separately.
Having placed water above the fire, one should place that food upon the water.
The vital breath itself, situated beneath the water, gently fans the fire.
The fire, being fanned by the wind, makes the water exceedingly hot.
That food is then cooked thoroughly on all sides with hot water.
When that is fully ripened, it becomes twofold: distinct and separate, with distinct flavors.
Torn apart by the twelve impurities, it becomes moist and departs from the body.
The ears, eyes, nose, tongue, teeth, penis, anus, and nails.
Phlegm and sweat are the seats of impurity; together with feces and urine, these are known as the twelve.
And all the channels are connected on every side to the heart-lotus.
That subtle vital breath places the essence within their mouths.
The vital breath (prāṇa) fills those channels again with that essence.
And being fully satisfied, they nourish the body on all sides.
Then that essence, situated within the channels of the body, [is heated] by the body's heat.
From that which is being cooked, two further types of cooking arise.
The skin becomes covered all over, and blood is produced.
From blood come the body hairs and the flesh; from the flesh come the hair of the head and the sinews.
From the sinews come the vessels and likewise the bones; from those, the marrow and then the nails.
The marrow produces the state of isolation (kaivalya) and the pure [semen], which is of the nature of procreation. || 45 ||
Thus, the twelvefold transformation of this [consciousness] has been proclaimed.
(Interpolation: From that very food [comes] the semen, and from the semen arises the body. Bindu is Śiva, rajas is Śakti; the moon is bindu, and the sun is rajas. || 46 ||
Only from the union of both is that which is designated as the *piṇḍa* obtained.
It is said that there are three mothers, three fathers, and three parts of Śiva.
Among those, the ninth part of the mixed totals is designated as the *piṇḍa*.
Blood and the state of flesh are known as the portions of the *mātṛkā*. || 48 ||
The bones, the channels, and the body hairs are proclaimed to be the portions of the ancestors (pitṛs).
Fire, wind, and the self are proclaimed to be portions of Śiva. || 49 ||
When, during the fertile period, the flawless semen has entered the womb;
Then, touched by that wind, it attains oneness with the female blood.
At the time of the emission of the semen, the living soul, joined with its instruments, [departs].
Impelled by his own past actions, he enters a womb with longing.
Due to the unification of that white and red [elements], the *kalala* comes into being within a single day.
Within five nights, the *kalala* shall attain the form of a bubble.
After seven nights it becomes a bubble, and after a month it becomes a peśī.
After two weeks, it becomes a *peśī*, firm and accumulated with blood and flesh.
Just as a sprout arises from a seed, [the result] appears after twenty-five nights.
And from that very knot, sprouts arise by means of a mere morsel of food. || 54 ||
The neck, the head, as well as the back, the two arms, the bones, and the belly;
Likewise the hands and feet, the armpits, the hips, and the limbs as well. || 55 ||
And within two months, all [the stages] arise in succession.
Within three months, all the limbs, sprouts, and joints are produced.
Within four months, the fingers are produced in their proper sequence.
Then the mouth, the nose, and the two ears are produced by the five [elements]. || 57 ||
Likewise, the rows of teeth are well-guarded, and the nails grow again.
Within six months, however, there will be holes in your ears.
The anus, the penis, the generative organ, and the navel are also produced.
And then, the joints that are produced in the limbs arise from those seven.
Complete with all major and minor limbs, and endowed with hair upon his head.
With his limbs clearly defined, he was further [endowed with beauty] over the course of eight months.
Endowed with the fivefold nature, it remains fully matured.
By the potency of the mother's food and by the sixfold taste. || 61 ||
By means of its connection to the umbilical cord, it grows day by day.
Then, when this little body has reached completion, the individual soul regains its memory.
One experiences pleasure and pain within sleep and dreams as a result of past actions.
Having died, I was born again; and having been born, I died again.
Thousands of various wombs have been seen by me since birth.
Now I have just been born, and I have already received my sacraments.
"Therefore, I shall perform that which will bring about welfare, by means of which my birth from a womb may occur."
While staying in the womb, he thinks thus: "Once I have emerged from the womb... (65)
Today I desire the knowledge of Śiva, which brings about the cessation of saṃsāra.
Thus, he was utterly tormented by the great suffering of the womb.
The individual soul, remaining under the sway of karma, should contemplate the means to liberation.
Just as someone oppressed by a great mountain remains in a state of suffering. || 67 ||
Likewise, old age again remains enveloped within the body amidst suffering.
Just as one who has fallen into the ocean remains there, overwhelmed by suffering. || 68 ||
With his limbs drenched by the amniotic fluid, the person is likewise distressed.
Just as someone placed in an iron cauldron is cooked by fire. || 69 ||
Likewise, cast into the vessel of the womb, it is cooked by the digestive fire.
Of one who is pierced incessantly by needles the color of fire; || 70 ||
Whatever suffering may arise, that within the womb becomes eightfold.
There is no dwelling anywhere more painful than dwelling in a womb.
For embodied beings, it is full of suffering, most terrible, and exceedingly perilous.
Thus has the dwelling in the womb been fully described for living beings. || 72 ||
Of all those things that move and are stable, according to their own internal nature.
The suffering from being crushed by the machine of the womb is ten million times greater than that of the embryo.
A state of fainting occurs for that embodied being as he is being born.
Just as sugarcane juice is being squeezed from all sides by a press, so it was for him.
Just as when one's head is being struck by the tips of hammers.
As he was emerging from the womb by means of powerful birth-winds, || 75 ||
Great suffering arises for one who finds no protection.
Just as sesame seeds and sugar-cane become devoid of essence when pressed by a machine, so too [are those who are oppressed].
In the same way, the body is substanceless, having been squeezed by the machinery of the womb.

(Likewise, in the Garbhopaniṣad: "There are six kinds of tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent. From taste comes blood; from blood, flesh; from flesh, fat; and from fat, the bones."
From the bones comes marrow; from marrow, semen; and from the union of semen and blood, the embryo develops.
He establishes it in the heart; within the heart is fire; in the place of fire is bile (*pitta*);
in the place of bile is wind (*vāyu*); and in the place of wind is the heart. Through the sequence of Prajāpati, there is the application [of the seed] at the time of the season.
After being retained for one night, it becomes the *kalala*; after being retained for seven nights, it becomes the *budbuda*;

within half a month, it becomes a mass (*piṇḍa*); within a month, it becomes solid; within two months, the head is formed; and within three months, the region of the feet is formed—in the sixth month.
In the seventh month, the mouth, nose, eyes, and ears are formed, and it becomes endowed with the life-force (jīva). In the eighth month, all its limbs become complete;
through an excess of the father's seed, it becomes male, and through an excess of the mother's seed, females are born.

Due to the equality of the seed of both [parents], a neuter being is born; when the minds are agitated, they become blind, lame, humpbacked, or dwarfish. From the flesh being oppressed by each other's vital winds (*vāyu*), semen and blood [are emitted]; from two women, twins—both male and female—are born in the womb. Then, in the ninth month...
He becomes endowed with all the primary marks; he remembers his former births; he knows the deeds performed and left unperformed; and he discerns both auspicious and inauspicious karma.
"Consequently, thousands of various wombs have indeed been seen by me."

Whatever wholesome or unwholesome karma has been performed by me for the sake of my own kin (or attendants), [may it bear fruit for them].
I am consumed by it all alone; they have departed as the sharers of the fruit.
For one who is born, there is death; and for one who has died, there is birth again and again.
Alas! Immersed in an ocean of suffering, I see no remedy.
If I am released from the womb, I shall take refuge in Maheśvara.
To him who brings about the destruction of impurity and bestows the fruit of liberation. || 80 ||

[The First Instruction, titled "The Procedure for the Origin of the Piṇḍa and the Wearing of the Liṅga," in the Dīkṣā Section of the Vīraśaivācārapradīpikā, compiled by Siddhadeva for the sake of enlightenment.]
[Thus ends the first chapter in the Śrīvīraśaivācārapradīpikā. || 1 ||
The Lamp of Vīraśaiva Conduct [Now the Second Chapter] | The Goddess said:
In this turbid age of Kali, which is difficult to conquer and hard to transcend.
When the conduct of the castes and stages of life had declined and social confusion had set in. || 1 ||
O Maheśvara, by what means are your devotees liberated?
The Lord said:
And he was submerged in the great heat within the wilderness of the suffering of saṃsāra.

now the mantra for the seat): [I meditate upon] Him who is in the form of a *liṅga*, beautifully tawny, radiant with the brilliance of blazing flames, shining intensely, and whose lotus-face is perfectly adorned and resplendent in the upper half of His single portion.

One should meditate upon that reality known as Mūrtisādākhya— the bestower of auspiciousness and fearlessness, attainable through meditation— which is endowed with three eyes, perfectly composed of limbs, and designated by the form of the Liṅga.
(The Mantra for the Installation of the Vessel:
He whose splendor is ruddy, rivaling the brilliance of gold blazing with the fire of universal dissolution and lightning;
who is known through the Sāmaveda with its deep resonance; and whose coppery lips are radiant—[to him, salutations].

The face of the Wielder of the Trident, with its three eyes, the crescent moon, and matted locks tawny like the lofty waves of the Gaṅgā—that is the Tatpuruṣa face, the eastern countenance bowed to by the lord of the gods. (30)
(The Tatpuruṣa Mantra: Oṃ, may we know that Tatpuruṣa; may we meditate upon Mahādeva; may Rudra impel us.
The mantra, which bestows that [attainment], is declared to be joined with the touching of the hand.
One should meditate upon those jyotirliṅgas and recollect the root five-syllabled mantra (mūla-pancākṣara). || 31 ||
One should also worship Viśveśa, the True Guru, and the face of Īśāna.
One should always remember the Lord, whose seed-syllable is the letter *ya*.
The root is indeed the five syllables; through this, there shall always be purity of touch.
(The Six-Syllable Mantra): Oṃ namaḥ śivāya. To Īśāna.
(Now, the Seat Mantra): In this great five-syllabled [mantra], may the peaceful-souled Lord Hīśvara, whose face is like a lotus, quickly grant his divine liṅga, which resembles a crystal gem.
He who dwells upon the five peaks.

One should meditate upon that auspicious and fearless Śiva-sādākhya-tattva, which is attainable through meditation, which bestows divine garments for an eon, and which grants a pair of glorious feet and staff-like arms. || 33 ||
(The Mantra for the Installation of the Vessel)

It is the stainless one, transcending the qualities of the manifest and the unmanifest, consisting of the thirty-six principles, the abode of the Vedas, the primordial syllable, and the mantra scriptures; it is to be meditated upon constantly by yogis.
Omniscience, supreme lordship, immovability, that which is subtler than the subtlest, and the peaceful fifth face of the Lord, consisting of pure light, are indeed to be served. || 34 ||
Thus, one should place the letter *ya* facing upwards [as the mantra]: "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām, īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānām, brahmādhipatirbrahmaṇo'dhipatirbrahmā śivo me astu sadāśivaḥ. This is the mantra.

(Then follows the purification with water from the jar: Oṃ! Water indeed is all this; water is all beings; water is the vital breaths; water is the cattle; water is food; water is immortality; water is the sovereign (*samrāj*); water is the universal ruler (*virāj*); water is the self-ruler (*svarāj*); water is the meters; water is the lights; water is the *yajus*-formulas; water is truth; water is everything.

The deities are the Waters. Having consecrated the water in the pitcher with the five Brahma-mantras beginning with *oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ sadyojāta*, one should then place jewels within those pitchers.
Pearl, ruby, sapphire, and coral;
One should cast both the *vajra* and the five [elements] into the [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta.
The Guru should sprinkle the ritual jars with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the products of the cow (gavya).
The most excellent of instructors should wrap each one with a new cloth.
One should place tufts made of nine blades of darbha grass within them. || 36 ||
For immediately after that, [he should do so] with five threads of the same kind as the thread of the cord.
One should encircle the five [objects] with threads resembling lattice windows.
Indeed, [he offered] sprouts of dūrvā grass, betel nuts, and leaves of the nāgavallī vine.
The bilva leaf, apāmārga leaves, and the dhātrī (tvapāmārga, tulasī, and dhātrī). || 38 ||
In initiation, these five auspicious [leaves] should be five-petaled.
One should place flowers such as the karavīra and others into the water-pots.
Having bathed and adorned himself with ornaments and garments, he likewise [honored] the officiating priests.
One should worship those four with flowers, unbroken grains of rice, sacred ash, and other such offerings. || 40 ||
The preceptor should perform the worship of Madhyama with flowers, unbroken rice grains, and other offerings.
The officiating priests, with delighted minds, should perform the worship of the other [deities]. || 41 ||
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth, as well as with incense and lamps.
The five types of food, fruits and so forth, plantains, and coconuts—42.
The worship of the Śiva-vessel,
as well as flour mixed with molasses, sesame seeds, and chickpeas.
And one should likewise worship the betel-roll in due order according to the prescribed rule.
One should place golden jewels and pearls within the jars. || 43 ||
The preceptor, on a sacrificial mound in the northeast direction, [should prepare] with grains of rice.
And one should perform [the rite] with sesame seeds, beautifully adorned and numbering according to what is prescribed in the scriptures. || 44 ||
Combined with the five precious gems, medicinal herbs, scented water, a bundle of kuśa grass, and so forth.
His neck was adorned with three threads, and his belly was anointed with sandalwood paste. || 45 ||
Covered with a pair of white garments and provided with flowers, perfumes, and unbroken grains of rice.
The auspicious water-pot, provided with fruit, a lid, and possessing the proper characteristics. || 46 ||
And in that pitcher, one should worship Śiva, mounted upon his bull, together with his limbs (attendants).
[Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Characteristics, Installation, and Worship of the Vessel," in the section on Initiation within the *Śrīvīraśaivācārapradīpikā*. || 5 ||
Salutations to the venerable gurus.
[Now the sixth chapter:
Now, the characteristics of the disciple,
as well as the procedure for the disciple's ritual bath, ornaments, and so forth, in their proper sequence.
And likewise, the Svastikārohaṇa and the Bhūtipada according to the prescribed ritual. || 1 ||
The ritual placement (nyāsa) of the five Brahmans and the wearing of rudrākṣa beads.
Listen, for I shall speak that which destroys the sins of those who hear it.
During the first part of the night, one should observe a fast and subsist on a diet of milk.
Having risen early the next morning, one should remember the lotus feet of the Guru.
Having performed his bath and purification, he should then put on a washed garment.
And one should wear ornaments, garlands, and ointments according to one's ability. || 4 ||
Having bestowed wealth upon the devotees of Śiva, preceded by the offering of betel leaf.
Having offered [the gifts] according to the sequence of seniority, one should worship them properly with flowers and other offerings.
Then, from all of them together, with the preeminent teacher at their head—
Having performed a circumambulation, one should offer betel with devotion.
Having approached and bowed at the feet of the teacher immediately thereafter, [he remained there].
One should worship with gold flowers and other offerings with devotion, according to one's means.
And having himself turned toward the east, he should smear [the ground] with cow dung.
The Guru should place the disciple within the mandala facing north.
And one should indeed cause the disciple to ascend the svastika by means of the mantra itself.
O Goddess, having gazed upon the disciple, the Guru should contemplate the reality (tattva).
The Ritual for Applying Ashes (The Mantra for Ascending the Svastika):
[This ash] arises from mud, is produced from the wood of the lotus, and is born of gold that severs the bonds existing outside.
Afterwards, the Guru, having composed himself, should become intent upon the lotus posture.
Having performed the binding of the foundation (ādhārabandhana), as well as exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka).
And having likewise performed the breath-retention (kumbhaka), preceded by meditation upon one's own guru.
Having meditated upon and mentally bowed to one's own guru within one's own heart.
And one should oneself perform the mudrā of the liṅga while reciting it together with the Praṇava.
Having meditated upon that five-syllabled [mantra], one should contemplate the invocation therein.
(In the Kāraṇatantra) ||
Having sprinkled ashes on the palm of the left hand and covered it with the other hand, the preceptor should apply the ash-mark (bhūtipaṭṭa) upon the disciple while reciting the mantra.
Having taken [the materials] with the mantras beginning with "Agni," one should sprinkle them upon the limbs.
The Bhūti-mantra: *Oṃ, fire is ashes, wind is ashes, water is ashes, earth is ashes, space is ashes;
indeed, all this is ashes. The mind and these senses are ashes.* This is the mantra for wearing [the ashes].
The Māna-mantra: *May there be no harm to our children, nor to our descendants, nor to our life, nor to our cattle, nor to our horses.*
Do not cause harm.

"O Rudra, may you not slay us in your wrathful state; we, possessing oblations, shall worship you with our minds. Thus. "Oṃ hrūṃ śiṃ, obeisance to Aghora," [recite] at the heart. "Oṃ hrīṃ maṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva."
In the secret place: Oṃ hrāṃ naṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta. In the two feet:
One should carefully scatter the fivefold ashes on the head in the Īśāna direction.
Fourfold on the face, eightfold with the Aghora mantra on the left [side], and likewise eightfold on the heart.
On the left, in the secret region, there are thirteen types.
With that same water, he should diligently wash his feet eight times.
One should thoroughly smear all the limbs with the Sadyojāta mantra according to the true principle.
(The Mantra for Massaging) (From the Pārameśvara Tantra): Homage to Bhava, to Rudra, to Śarva, to Ugra, and to Śambhu.
"Namo vibhūtirūpāya siddharūpāya te namaḥ"— having thus rubbed the sacred ash mixed with water [on the body],
[one should apply it] to the head, the forehead, the two ears, the neck, and the two arms.
The chest, the navel, the back, and the hump—these are among the eleven [sites].
One should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with the Tryambaka mantra and the Triyāyus mantra.
Oṃ, we worship the three-eyed one, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity.
"May I be liberated from death, as a cucumber from its stem, but not from immortality.
The triple life-span of Jamadagni, the triple life-span of Kaśyapa, the triple life-span of Agastya, and that which is the triple life-span of the gods—may that triple life-span be mine. (19)

With this mantra, one should apply the *tripuṇḍra* on the head, forehead, both ears, throat, both arms, chest, navel, and the back. (Then follows the ritual placement on the hands): *Oṃ Oṃ Oṃ* salutation to the two thumbs; *Oṃ Naṃ Oṃ* salutation to the two index fingers; *Oṃ Maṃ Oṃ*.
Oṃ *ma* Oṃ, salutation to the two middle fingers. Oṃ *śiṃ* Oṃ, salutation to the two ring fingers. Oṃ *vāṃ* Oṃ, salutation to the two little fingers. Oṃ *yaṃ* Oṃ, salutation to the hands.
This is the procedure for the ritual placement (*aṅganyāsa*) upon the limbs.
Salutation to the palms and backs of the hands. Thus is the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa).
(Now, the six-limbed assignment: Oṃ hrāṃ oṃ, salutation to the heart, the abode of all powers.
Oṃ hrauṃ naṃ, svāhā to the head, the abode of the power of satisfaction.
Oṃ hrūṃ maṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhā) which is the abode of the power of primordial awakening.
Oṃ hraiṃ śiṃ, to the abode of the independent power (svatantra-śakti), for the armor, huṃ!
Oṃ hrīṃ vaṃ, to the abode of unimpeded power, to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ!
Oṃ hraḥ yaṃ, phaṭ! To the weapon [mantra] residing in the abode of infinite power.

Having thus performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*): *oṃ yaṃ hraḥ oṃ phaṭ*, obeisance to Īśāna on the head; *oṃ vāṃ rauṃ ai vauṣaṭ*, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa on the mouth; *oṃ śiṃ haiṃ uṃ huṃ*, obeisance to Aghora on the heart; *oṃ maḥ hrūṃ iṃ vaṣaṭ*, obeisance to Vāmadeva on the private parts.
Having performed the Nyāsa of the Five Brahmans as follows: at the secret place (guhya), "Oṃ naṃ hiṃ Oṃ svāhā, obeisance to Sadyojāta"; and at the two feet, [the same].
Then, having performed the placement of the five syllables beginning with *ya* and ending with *na* on the head, forehead, throat, heart, and navel;
Then follows the placement of the Kalās (kalānyāsa): *Oṃ*, obeisance to Īśāna, the Lord of all sciences, and to Śaśinī; [this is placed] on the head.
Oṃ, the Lord of all beings; salutation to Him and to Aṅgadā on the eastern head. Oṃ, the overlord of Brahmā, the overlord of the sacred word; salutation to Him and to Jyeṣṭhā on the southern head.
Oṃ, may Brahmā be auspicious to me; homage to him and to Marīci. [On the left head.]
Oṃ Sadāśivoṃ; salutation to Him and to Jvālinī on the western head.
Oṃ, we know that Tatpuruṣa; salutation to Him and to Peace in the eastern face.
Oṃ, we meditate upon Mahādeva; salutation to him and to that Vidyā, in the right face.
Oṃ, salutation to Rudra, to him, and to the installation; [this is] on the left face.
Oṃ pracodayāt; salutation to that Nivṛtti in the western face.
Oṃ, homage to the face of Īśāna, located in the upward-facing direction.
Oṃ, obeisance to the non-terrible ones; obeisance to Tamasī in the heart.
Oṃ, now, obeisance to the Terrifying One and to the Enchanting One at the throat.
Oṃ, salutation to Ghorākṣayā on the right shoulder.
Oṃ, to those most terrible and more terrible than the terrible, salutation to Kaniṣṭhā on the left shoulder.
Oṃ, salutation to all [deaths], from everywhere, to every death; [place this] at the navel.
Oṃ, salutation to Māyā, who is all-in-all; [this is for] the belly.
Oṃ, salutation be to you, O Rudra; salutation for fearlessness on the back.
Oṃ, obeisance to the auspicious forms, to Jvarā, on the chest;
Oṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva, obeisance to Rajā, on the private parts.
Oṃ, obeisance to the Eldest; obeisance to the Protector at the Liṅga.
Oṃ, homage to the most excellent; homage to the generative organs; homage to the testicles.
Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra, obeisance to Rati; [this is for] the right thigh.
Oṃ, salutation to Kāla; salutation to Pālyā on the left thigh.
Oṃ, salutation to Kalavikaraṇī; salutation to Buddhi at the right knee.
Oṃ, salutation to Balā; salutation to Kārayitrī on the left knee.
Oṃ, salutation to Balavikaraṇa; salutation to Buddhi on the right calf.
Oṃ, salutation to Balapramathana; salutation to Dhātrī on the left calf.
Oṃ, salutation to Balavikaraṇī on the right hip.
Oṃ, salutation to the Lord of the Pramathas; salutation to Dhātrī at the left hip.
Oṃ, homage to the Subduer of All Beings; homage to the Village Leader on the waist.
Oṃ, salutation to Manamohinī on the right side.
Oṃ, obeisance to Unmanā; obeisance to Tamomohā. On the left side.
Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutation to Siddhi on the right foot.
Oṃ, salutation indeed to Sadyojāta; salutation to Buddhi; salutation to the left foot.
Oṃ, obeisance to the messenger Bhavā in the right hand.
The procedure for the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*):
*Oṃ abhave lakṣmyai namaḥ* on the left hand.
Oṃ, salutation to Anātibhavā for the sake of intelligence, in the nose.
Oṃ bhajasva māṃ kāṃtyai namaḥ on the head.
Oṃ bhava, salutation to Svadhā on the right arm.
Oṃ, salutation to Udbhava; salutation to Dhṛti on the left arm.
Thus, having elaborated upon the ritual placement of the *kalās*.
Then, that most excellent teacher should perform the invocation of those kalās for the disciple.
Having avoided a lump of meat, one should instead prepare a lump of mantra.

Then the preceptor, having placed a heap of *rudrākṣa* beads upon a washed cloth, consecrated them with this mantra: "Oṃ hrūṃ srūṃ rūṃ jrūṃ prāṃ rūm api śrīṃ maṃ kṣāṃ kṣam api krāṃ kṣāṃ hūṃ namaḥ," and having performed the eightfold worship (*aṣṭavidhārcanapūjā*), thereafter—
To the seed of the rudrākṣa tree, the cause of the origin of sacred ash.
Salutations to Rudra, the three-eyed one, who seeks the welfare of the world. || 21 ||
Having thus paid homage, one should then wear [the respective items] on those specific locations with their respective mantras.

Oṃ, salutation to the illustrious Sadāśiva. At the crest [of the head], one face with one mouth. "Oṃ, salutation to the illustrious Śiva, the lord of fire, sun, and moon"—with this [mantra], three faces each, totaling twelve, [are assigned] to the head.
"Oṃ, salutation to the venerable Paraśiva, who consists of the thirty-six principles"—
with this, one should place eleven faces, one on each head.
"Oṃ somāya namaḥ"—with this, one should worship the fifteen faces, each with six [offerings], and the two ears.
Oṃ, salutation to Śrīkaṇṭha, the three-eyed one, whose essence is Time; [there are] thirty-six faces on the throat.
Oṃ, salutation to the illustrious Sarvajña, whose essence consists of the forms beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha.
Fifty garlands of four-faced [beads] are upon his chest.
Oṃ, salutation to Śrīkaṇṭha, who consists of the sixteen forms beginning with Sukhāsana;
he has thirteen faces and sixteen arms each.
Oṃ, salutation to the illustrious Somanātha, whose essence is the digit of the moon; [there are] nine faces and twelve [fingers] on each of the two wrists.
Oṃ, homage to the illustrious Mahādeva, who is presided over by the twelve Ādityas; [this is for] the armpits.

Oṃ, obeisance to the illustrious Lord of Umā, who is the presiding deity of the forms beginning with Keśava; one hundred and eight [offerings] for the fourteen faces in the place of the sacred thread.
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Viśveśvara, whose essence is the Lord of Knowledge of the Hundred Rudras; one should perform this at the binding of the forty-five-fold belly.

"Oṃ, obeisance to the Lord of the sixty-four arts; Oṃ Hīṃ, obeisance to Śrī Umāpati, the Self of all, who has become the source of birth and whose form consists of all the arts. Thus one should perform the wearing of Rudrākṣa beads.

[Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Initiation of the Disciple, Beginning with the Bath, Adornment, Drawing the Svastika, Wearing the Vibhūti, and the Nyāsa of the Five Brahmans, as well as the Characteristics and the Procedure for Wearing Rudrākṣas," in the Śrīvīraśaivācārapradīpikā, within the Section on Initiation.]
Salutations to the venerable gurus.
[Now begins the seventh chapter:
The determination of the substances required for worship and the sequence of the ritual adoration.
I shall describe the characteristics of nyāsa; listen, O you who are devoted to me.
And likewise, the cow-dung, urine, curd, milk, and ghee of cows.
And having placed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in separate vessels, one by one.
O Īśānī, milk is in the center, and curd is said to be in the east of that.
Having placed ghee on the south and likewise cow-dung on the north;
In the west, one should likewise place urine and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
(In the Kriyāsāra:
five prasthas and likewise five kuḍavas for each [ingredient].
And one *kuḍava* each; in its absence, *nikuñjana*. || 4 ||
In this manner, the most excellent preceptor should cause the mobile liṅga to be fashioned. || 5 ||
Milk, curd, and ghee, as well as honey together with sugar.
In the west, one should likewise place sugar; these are the presiding deities of the five Brahmās.
One should perform the rites as beautifully as possible with bells and the five great musical instruments.
The worshipper should always keep the top of the liṅga from being empty.
Oṃ hraiṃ, salutation to Tatpuruṣa; hauṃ haṃ khaṃ maṃ kṣaṃ taṃ yaṃ maṃ, and thereafter, salutation to Śiva.
With this mantra, that best of preceptors should perform [the rite] upon the body of the disciple.
(The materials for the *arghya* offering:
tips of *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, white mustard seeds, barley, rice, and milk.
The eminent sages declare these six substances to constitute the arghya offering.
Siddhārtha, kuṅkuma, dūrvā, koṣṭha, lāmañjaka, and śaśi.
And here, these six substances are said to constitute the water for washing the feet (pādya).
Phala, kacora, karpūra, koṣṭha, kāśmīra, and elaka;
They declare these six substances to be for the purpose of sipping water (ācamanīya).
The arghya, pādya, ācamana, and prokṣaṇa constitute the fourfold [offering]. || 11 ||

(The mantras are distinct: (The Arghya Mantra: *Oṃ devādevebhyo arghayante viśvāya devāya svadhāgne.* To the God of gods, to the Universal God, [I offer] the arghya; [it is] with *svadhā*, O Agni. To the Universal God who has come together from all sides, whose hands are everywhere... (Then the Pādya Mantra: *Pādo'sya viśvābhūtāni tripādasyāmṛtaṃ divi.* One foot of Him is all beings; His three feet are the immortal in heaven.
The Puruṣa rose up, three-quarters of him being above; one-quarter of him came into existence here again. To this foot [of the Puruṣa], Svāhā! (This is the water for washing the feet.)
Arghya, Svāhā! (Then the water for sipping: Oṃ, Rudra, the great seer, is all-pervading like a razor and has faces on every side; he transcends the universe.
Salutation to Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna; [this is] the water for sipping, svāhā.
Then, having performed an oil massage, especially upon the pedestal of the Liṅga.
(Now, regarding the five products of the cow: Cow urine with the Sadyojāta mantra, and cow dung with the Vāmadeva mantra.
And milk with the Aghora mantra, and curd with the Tatpuruṣa mantra.
One should offer ghee with the Īśāna mantra and [the other substances] with the Sadyojāta and other mantras. Thus ends the bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
The mantra: Oṃ hrāṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta; cow’s urine, svāhā! Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva; cow dung, svāhā!
The Ritual for Bathing with the Five Nectars:
Oṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to Aghora; cow’s ghee, svāhā!
Oṃ hraiṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa; curd, svāhā!
Oṃ hrauṃ, obeisance to Īśāna; cow’s milk, svāhā! Thus is the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Next, I shall describe the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), which bestows all prosperity upon men.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before Śiva with rice measuring one droṇa.
Having drawn a lotus in the center with eight petals and a pericarp.
One should place five vessels in the five central and other compartments.
Milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, and sugar—this is the pentad.
This is declared to be the five nectars (pañcāmṛta); one should place each in its own separate vessel.
One should worship the presiding deities of the stomach for each individual vessel.
Ambikā, Gaṇāmbā, Gaṅgā, Gaurī, and Manonmanā.
She should be worshipped by the best of the twice-born with offerings beginning with milk and ending with sugar.
Among the items beginning with milk and ending with sugar, [one should offer] each separately in their respective intervals.
One should perform the ritual bath with the five mantras beginning with Sadyojāta.
The mortal who acts in this way shall attain a meritorious state. || 19 ||
The minister, having prepared the Rudrapada according to the rules, should fill it with milk for the Moon (Vidhu), with curd for Indra (Devendra),
with fresh ghee for the Son of Bhrigu (Bhānuja), and with extracted honey for Soma (Saumya).
O Bhō, one should place sugar stirred with water in the west, the dhātrī fruit in the southeast and the southwest, well-ground [grain] in the northwest,
and kuśa grass in the northeast.
Now, the mantra for milk.
Swell up for me; let there be virility in you from all sides, O Soma, in the gathering of strength.

"Oṃ, salutation to [the deity] together with his limbs, together with his weapons, together with his retinue, together with his vehicle, together with all ornaments, and together with his power. With this mantra, one should bathe [the deity] with milk. Then, one should perform the water bath using the very same Īśāna mantra.

Then follows the mantra of Īśāna: *Oṃ īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānāṃ brahmādhipatir brahmaṇo'dhipatir brahmā śivo me astu sadāśivaḥ oṃ*. With this mantra, one performs the bath with pure water for each [deity] individually.

One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and the like, as well as unbroken grains (akṣata) and so forth. Oṃ hraiṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa—thus [offering] the sacred ash (bhasma). Oṃ hrāṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to Īśāna—the garment (vastra). Oṃ hreṃ, huṃ, obeisance to Kavaca—the sacred thread (upavīta). Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva—the perfume (gandha). Oṃ hrūṃ, phaṭ, obeisance to Astra.
Unbroken grains. *Oṃ namaḥ śivāya*—flower. *Oṃ hraṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*—incense. *Oṃ hreṃ kavacāya huṃ*—lamp. *Oṃ namaḥ śivāya*—food offering (*naivedya*).
*Oṃ namaḥ śivāya*—water for drinking. *Oṃ hruṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*.
Sugandhadravyayuktaśītodakaṃ svāhā. Oṃ namaḥ śivāya anulepanaṃ svāhā. Oṃ hraiṃ tatpuruṣāya namaḥ tāmbūlaṃ. Oṃ hrau haṃ hauṃ haṃ saṃ ābharaṇaṃ svāhā. Oṃ namaḥ śivāya darpaṇaṃ. Oṃ namaḥ śivāya.
The sound of the bell: in this manner, one should perform the worship with the respective mantra for each.
Now follows the mantra for the bath with curd.
The Ritual for Bathing with the Five Nectars (Pañcāmṛta-snāna-vidhi):
Oṃ, I have celebrated Dadhikrāvan, the victorious, the spirited horse. May he make our mouths fragrant;
may he prolong our lives. Oṃ, [this is offered] to the one who possesses his limbs, his weapons, and his retinue.
"Salutation to the one with his vehicle, adorned with all ornaments, and accompanied by his power (Śakti)"—with this, I bathe [the deity] with curd.
One should perform the water-bath using the very same *tatpuruṣa* mantra: "Oṃ, we know that Tatpuruṣa;
we meditate upon Mahādeva; may that Rudra inspire us. Thus is the water-bath.
Then, one should perform the worship according to the manner previously described.
Now follows the bath with clarified butter.

Oṃ, you are white, you are light, you are splendor; may the divine Savitṛ purify you with the flawless purifier, with the rays of the sun, the Vasu. Oṃ, salutation to [the deity] together with his limbs, together with his weapons, together with his retinue, together with his vehicle, adorned with all ornaments, and endowed with power—thus, with ghee.

I bathe [thee]. One should perform the water-bath with the Aghora mantra alone: "Oṃ, to those who are non-terrible and to those who are terrible, and to those more terrible than the terrible—salutations be unto thee in thy forms as Rudra. Thus is the water-bath.
One should perform the worship according to the manner previously described.
Now follows the mantra for the honey-bath.
Oṃ. Sweet are the winds for the one who follows the cosmic order; sweet flow the rivers. May the plants be sweet for us.
Sweet be the night and sweet the dawn. Sweet be the earthly realm. May the sky, our father, be sweet;
may the lord of the forest be full of sweetness; may the sun be full of sweetness. May the cows be sweet for us.

Oṃ, salutation to [the deity] together with his limbs, together with his weapons, together with his retinue, together with his vehicle, adorned with all ornaments, and endowed with power; thus, I bathe him with honey.
One should perform the ritual bath with water using the Vāmadeva mantra: *Oṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ, jyeṣṭhāya namaḥ, śreṣṭhāya namaḥ,
rudrāya namaḥ, kālāya namaḥ, kalavikaraṇāya namaḥ, balāya namaḥ.*

"Salutation to the transformer of power; salutation to the subduer of power; salutation to the tamer of all beings; salutation to the one who transcends the mind"—with these [mantras], one performs the bath with water.
Then, one should perform the worship according to the manner previously described.
Now, the mantra for bathing with sugar: Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ; we meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ.

"May He who impels our intellects [grant us wisdom]. With "Oṃ, salutation to [the Deity] together with His limbs, together with His weapons, together with His retinue, together with His vehicle, adorned with all ornaments, and endowed with His power," one should offer the bath of sugar.

One should perform a water bath with the *sadyojāta* mantra: "Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations, salutations to Sadyojāta. In existence, in non-existence, and beyond existence—be present for me! Salutations to Bhavodbhava. Thus one should perform the bath with pure water. Then, according to the previously mentioned method...
One should perform the worship: *Oṃ yāḥ phalinīryā aphalā apuṣpā yāśca puṣpiṇīḥ*.
"May those [waters] impelled by Bṛhaspati release us from sin.
Oṃ, salutations to the one who is with his limbs, with his weapons, with his retinue, with his vehicle, adorned with all ornaments, and endowed with power;
thus I bathe you with water and fruit. One should perform the water-bath with the Triyaṃbaka mantra.
We worship the three-eyed one, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity.
"May I be released from death, as a cucumber from its stalk, into immortality"—with this, one performs the bath with pure water.

Then, one should perform worship according to the previously mentioned method. One who worships Śiva with true devotion should especially rub [the linga] with a powder of barley and wheat, or with a powder of mung beans, while reciting the mantra "Mayi medhām," and then bathe the linga with lukewarm water.
Now, the mantra for lukewarm water: "May Agni bestow wisdom upon me, progeny upon me, and splendor upon me.
With this mantra, one should perform the bath with lukewarm water. Then: *Oṃ hroṃ īśānāya namaḥ*, I bathe [the deity] with scented water. *Oṃ hraiṃ tatpuruṣāya*... [and so forth].
The Ritual for the Worship of the Vessel (*kalaśapūjanavidhi*):
With "Namaḥ," [I offer] water with flowers; with "Svāhā," [I offer] water. With "Oṃ Hrūṃ Aghorāya Namaḥ," I bathe [the deity] with golden water.
With "Oṃ Hrīṃ Vāmadevāya Namaḥ," I bathe [the deity] with jewel-water. With "Oṃ Hrāṃ... [I bathe with water].
"Salutation to Sadyojāta; I bathe [the deity] with water consecrated by the root mantra: Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ hraḥ.
Thus I bathe [the deity] with coconut water."
Next is the procedure for the ritual ablution with the water of sacred fords (tīrtha).
(Now, the mantra for the meditation on the water-pot: Rudra resides at the mouth of the pot, and Viṣṇu is established at its neck.
Brahmā is situated at its base, and the hosts of Mothers are remembered as being in the middle.
Within his belly were all the oceans and the earth with its seven continents.
But all the remaining deities are indeed supported by the water-pot.
"The waters of all oceans and all auspicious sacred fords"—this is the visualization.
Then (the invocation mantra): O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, please be present in this water.

Then, having consecrated the water with the previously mentioned mantra "oṃ āpaḥ," one should worship the pitcher with ash, sandalwood paste, and other offerings. (The measurement of the pitcher): According to the *Kāraṇāgama*, for the bathing of a mobile liṅga, five āḍhakas of water are required.
The most excellent of gurus should also bathe [the image] with even five prasthas [of water]. || 21 ||
The mobile liṅga is for one's own benefit, while the fixed liṅga is for the benefit of others.
Eight horizontal barley grains or three vertical rice grains [constitute the measure]. || 22 ||
This is declared to be the measure of a finger; such is the definition of a finger.
It should be six finger-breadths wide and twelve finger-breadths long.
This is declared to be the measure of a *prastha* by those learned in the Vedas and the Shastras.
The preceptor should properly worship the water-pot with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
The Guru should then consecrate Śiva with the water contained within the Śiva-kumbha.
Having understood the yoga of the nature of the vital breaths, one should perform the ritual installation.
Prāṇa is declared to be the mantra, while Prakṛti is said to be the mūrti.
Having understood the vital breath (prāṇa) and the form of primordial nature (prakṛti), one should perform the rite of installation.
And the conjunction of the mantra and the image is the cause for the presence of Śiva.
One should likewise install the mantras for the infusion of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) and the phonemes representing the constituent parts (kalās).
That which is the supreme, most subtle aspect of mantras, the ultimate awakener.
Having drawn it forth according to the rule, one should properly install it upon the liṅga.
With the root mantra, one should place that hand of Śiva upon the head of Śiva.
Reciting "Oṃ, this hand of mine is the Blessed One," one who knows the digits of *nāda* and *bindu* should place them in their respective locations;
*nāda* is declared to be the *liṅga*, and *bindu* is said to be *śakti*.
But the digit (kalā) and Gomukha are designated as the station (sthāna). || 30 ||
Now follows the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
Oṃ hrāṃ, homage to the heart. Oṃ naṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the head. Oṃ maṃ hrūṃ, vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock. Oṃ śiṃ hraiṃ, huṃ to the armor. Oṃ vāṃ hrauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes.
The nature of the five-syllable mantra is *oṃ yaṃ hraḥ*; the six-limbed mantra is *astrāya phaṭ*.
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ hraḥ; this is the mantra of the limbs of Śiva.
Oṃ hraṃ hrauṃ haṃ saṃ; this is the mantra of the fivefold expansion.
The five-syllable mantra is "namaḥ śivāya" (Salutation to Śiva).
Oṃ namaḥ śivāya—this is the root five-syllable mantra.
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ namaḥ śivāya is the gross five-syllabled mantra.
Oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ śivāya—this is the subtle five-syllabled mantra.
Oṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ namaḥ śivāya—this is the five-syllable mantra known as Māyā.
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ namaḥ śivāya—this is the five-syllable mantra of grace (prasāda).
Oṃ hraḥ, to the abode of infinite power, whose form is light, the weapon of Śiva, phaṭ—
this is the mantra of the Śiva-weapon.
Oṃ āṃ īṃ ūṃ, to the one who pervades the sky, to the sky-weapon, phaṭ—thus is the mantra of the sky-weapon.
"Oṃ paśu haṃ phaṭ"—this is the Pāśupata weapon mantra; one should contemplate it within the center of the *liṅga* together with the previously mentioned placement of the *kalās*.
A linga consecrated with seven crores of great mantras is so described.
The mantra is the form of the deity; Śiva consists of the very nature of the mantra. || 31 ||
All activities, such as plowing and so forth, are declared to be performed by means of mantra alone.
Having understood this, the practitioner of mantra should perform worship; otherwise, it will be fruitless. || 32 ||
Then follows the mantra for the installation of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhāpanamantra).
Oṃ. For this Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra, the meters are the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva;
the deity is the Vital Energy (Prāṇa-śakti) who creates the entire universe; the seed-syllable is AṂ;
the power is HRĪṂ; the pin is KROṂ. [This is employed] for the purpose of establishing all mantras in this place.
The application.

Oṃ iṃ īṃ jhaṃ jaṃ chaṃ caṃ śaṃ Ūrdhvakeśinī, svāhā to the head! Aṃ ṇaṃ ḍhaṃ ḍaṃ ṭhaṃ ṭaṃ uṃ Jaṃṭinī Śikhinī Padmāntarvartinī, vauṣaṭ to the self of the ears, eyes, nose, skin, and tongue! To the crest-lock (śikhā), vauṣaṭ!
To the self of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals:
Oṃ Aiṃ Naṃ Dhaṃ Daṃ Thaṃ Taṃ, to the armor of Māyā residing in the three worlds, Huṃ; [the powers of] speaking, moving, grasping, excreting, and experiencing bliss.

Oṃ, to the self of earth, water, fire, air, and ether; Oṃ Aṃ Jiṃ Ghaṃ Khaṃ Kaṃ Āṃ, salutation to the heart of Saṃjīvanī, the self of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; Oṃ Oṃ Maṃ Bhaṃ Baṃ Phaṃ Paṃ Oṃ, to the intermediate spaces and the three eyes, vauṣaṭ.

To the self consisting of mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness: Oṃ kṣaṃ haṃ saṃ ṣaṃ śaṃ vaṃ laṃ raṃ yaṃ, to the weapon for slaying, phaṭ! Aṃ hrīṃ kroṃ, yaralavaśaṣasa, ho haṃ kṣaṃ, transcending all together: here is the vital breath (prāṇa) of such-and-such; here is the life-force (jīva) of such-and-such; here is the life-force of such-and-such; here is the stability of such-and-such.

"May all the sense organs of this one—his mind, eyes, tongue, nose, skin, breath, fire, and wind—abide; svāhā! Having performed the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) with this mantra, [then follows] the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the letters of the alphabet (*mātṛkā*).
The letters *a* and *ā* are at the crown and the forehead; *i* and *ī* are in the right and left eyes; *u* and *ū* are in the right and left ears; *ṛ* and *ṝ* are in the right and left cheeks;
*ḷ* and *ḹ* are in the right and left nostrils; and *e* and *ai*—
The vowels *o* and *au* are on the upper and lower lips. *Aṃ* and *aḥ* are on the two palates. The five letters beginning with *ka* are on the five fingers of the right hand;
the five letters beginning with *ca* are on the fingers of the left hand; and the five letters beginning with *ta* [are on the fingers of the right foot].
On the toes of the right and left feet;
the rule for the worship of the limbs of Hara is as follows:
the letter *pa* is on the abdomen; the letters *pha* and *ba* are on the right and left sides; the letter *bha* is on the shoulder.
The letter *ma* is in the heart; the letters beginning with *ya* and ending with *sa* are in the seven constituents (dhātus) starting with the skin;

the letter *ha* is in the self (*ātman*); and the letter *kṣa* is in the anger directed toward the enemies that are the births and so forth of the worshippers. In this manner, one should meditate upon these letters of the Mātṛkā within the center of the *liṅga*.

Then follows the bath. With this mantra, "Oṃ hrāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ," one should offer the water for the guest-offering (arghya), the water for washing the feet (pādya), and the water for sipping (ācamanīya). Then, having performed the worship according to the previously mentioned method, one should present the articles of worship with their respective mantras.
Then follows the worship of the limbs.
Oṃ, salutation to Hara; I worship the feet.
Salutation to Śambhu; I worship the two ankles.
Homage to Śubhā; I worship the two knees.
Homage to Sarvanivāsa; I worship the thighs.
Homage to the support of all; I worship the hips.
Homage to Sarvarakṣā; I worship the hips.
Salutation to the one clothed in space; I worship the center.
Salutation to Nakṣatramālī; I worship the navel.
Salutation to Sarveśvara; I worship the belly.
Salutation to Umākānta; I worship the chest.
Salutation to Nīlakaṇṭha; I worship the throat.
Salutation to the destroyer of Tripura; I worship the arms.
Salutation to Śaṅkara; I worship my hands.
Salutation to Vṛṣa; I worship the exterior of the throat.
Salutation to the bestower of the fruits of sacrifice; I worship the mouth.
Homage to Nāgahārā; I worship the nose.
Salutation to the one whose eyes are Indra, Arka, and Vahni; I worship the eyes.
Salutation to Kapālin; I worship the forehead.
I worship the two ears with "Salutation to Phaṇikuṇḍala."
Homage to Gaṅgādhara; I worship the matted locks.
Salutation to Somabhūṣaṇa; I worship Kaparda.
Salutation to Śubhadā; I worship [her] with all my limbs.
Thus is the worship (followed by the offering of flowers): obeisance to the god Bhava; obeisance to the god Śarva;
obeisance to the god Rudra; obeisance to the god Paśupati; obeisance to the god Ugra; obeisance to the god Mahat; obeisance to the god Bhīma; obeisance to Īśāna.
One should offer flowers with this mantra, "Salutation to the God," or with the one hundred and eight names of Śiva, or with the thousand names.
(Now, the characteristics of the ten ingredients: Black aloe-wood, sandalwood, guggulu, and white aloe-wood;
Lac, bilva fruit, ghee, honey, sarjarasa, and camphor; || 33 ||
"O Four-faced One, the means for incense consist of ten ingredients."
"Oṃ hrāṃ to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ"—with this, [offer] incense, svāhā.
"Oṃ hraiṃ to the armor, huṃ"—with this, [offer] the lamp, svāhā.
With the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya," ending with svāhā and using the banner mudrā, [offer] the food offering (naivedya).
Svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva—thus [offering] water for drinking, Svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to the heart—thus [offering] water for sipping, Svāhā!
"Oṃ namaḥ śivāya," with this [mantra] one offers unguent, svāhā;
"Oṃ hraiṃ tatpuruṣāya namaḥ," with this [mantra] one offers betel, svāhā.
[This is] the description of the manner of praying to Śiva.
With the mantra *oṃ hraṃ hrauṃ hraṃ hrauṃ haṃ saṃ*, [one should offer] the ornaments, *svāhā*.
With the mantra *oṃ namaḥ śivāya*, one should show the mirror and fan with chowries.
[In the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā, it says: [One should worship] Śiva with worldly and Vedic hymns.
One should offer praise according to one's own ability.
Then, displaying the conch mudrā, [one should say]: "May there be success for us both."
With palms joined in reverence, one should pray to the God: "Be eternally established here. (34)
Having thus addressed the Lord of Gods, one should likewise offer a handful of flowers.
Thousands of offenses are committed by me day and night.
Protect me from my transgressions, as a father protects his beloved son.
Having thus offered the mantra-flowers.
Then: "And whatever fruit of worship there may be, one should cause all of it to be bestowed by means of water. (36)
Forming the añjali mudrā by contracting the four fingers of the right hand.
Having taken the flower and water, one should let them flow from the little finger onto the ground.
This would be but a small amount of water at the soles of one's own feet. || 38 ||
[Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Section on Initiation," in the *Śrīvīraśaivācārapradīpikā*.]
Homage to the venerable gurus.
[Now begins the eighth chapter]:
The worship of the disciple’s hands, as well as [the worship] of his hands and head.
The conjunction itself, as well as the establishment of the six chakras in that very same manner. || 1 ||
I shall now explain the sequence of the instruction on the mantra, as follows:
The locations for wearing the *liṅga*, as well as bathing and the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite. || 2 ||
With the thumb of the left hand and with perfume, one should [draw] the mandala on the right hand.
Having performed that, one should worship the Lord there, together with the seat, the ancillary limbs, and so forth.
One should utter the Śiva-mantra over the hand, which is composed of the splendor of Śiva.
"This hand of mine is the Blessed One; this [other] hand of mine is the even more Blessed One."
This is my universal medicine; this is the auspicious touch.
This is my mother, this is my father; this life-giver has arrived.
This crawling of yours has been brought about by Subandhu and Nirahni.
First, one should perform the consecration with the five-syllabled mantra alone.
With flowers, perfumes, unbroken grains, incense, lamps, food offerings, and mantras.
It is said that [the soul] knows by means of the pretext of the contact between the hand and the head.
Then, having formed the Śivahasta mudrā, he should place it upon the head of the disciple.
One should place that mantra on the region of the heart with the [right] hand, and likewise upon the head with the thumb alone.
The name of the agent is "equal fingers," and the name of the action is "both hands."
One should offer perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, betel leaves, and so forth.
Then, one should place the syllables upon the petals of the six cakras, beginning with the Ādhāra.
One should place the Sadyojāta [face], the earth element, the seed-syllable *na*, the four-petaled lotus, with Brahmā as its presiding deity, the Ācāra-liṅga, and the Ādhāra-cakra at the anus.
One should describe the location and other details of the Ādhāra-cakra;
[one should know] Vāmadeva as its presiding authority (āpta), the seed-syllable *ma*, Viṣṇu as its presiding deity (adhidaivata), and the six-petaled Guru-liṅga.
In the Svādhiṣṭhāna-cakra, located at the site of the liṅga, one should establish the syllables *bha, ma, ya, ra, la, va*.

One should establish the non-terrible (aghora) fire-principle, whose seed-syllable is Śika-ra, as the Śiva-liṅga with ten petals, presided over by Rudra, in the Maṇipūraka at the location of the navel.

One should establish in the heart the Tatpuruṣa aspect of the air element (vāyutatva), which has the seed-syllable *va*, is presided over by Īśvara, consists of twelve petals, is a mobile liṅga, contains the consonants from *ka* to *ṭha*, and is the Anāhata-cakra.

One should place at the throat the Īśāna principle, which is the element of space (ākāśatattva), has the seed-syllable *ya*, is presided over by Sadāśiva, consists of sixteen petals, is the Prasāda-liṅga, and is the Viśuddhi-cakra of the first sixteen vowels.

One should establish in the middle of the eyebrows the two-petaled Ājñā-cakra, whose seed-syllable is Praṇava, which is the Great Liṅga, the principle of the mind (manas-tattva), and whose essence consists of the Śrī-guru, Haṃ, Kṣa, and the Self (ātman).
That mantra which is uttered by the Guru into one's ear is called the *karṇa-mantra*.
The Guru should teach, in sequence, the seed-syllable, the phoneme, the vowel, and the power.
The letter *na* is to be known as the earth, while the letter *ma* is held to be the waters.
The syllable ŚI is declared to be fire, and the syllable VA is said to be wind.
For space (ākāśa) is indeed the letter *ya*; thus it is remembered as the five-syllabled [mantra].
But that disciple, with palms joined in reverence, had his mind entirely intent upon the mantra.
The disciple should conduct himself slowly, according to the instruction of the Śivācārya.
And when he has been purified by mantras, the Guru reveals the Liṅga to him.
Therefore, O Goddess, the disciple is known as "liṅgāyita. || 10 ||
Having cut his bonds with a sharp knife, one should point toward the *liṅga*.
The scissors are the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), by which he cuts the bonds. || 11 ||
Indeed, once the body of the disciple has been purified by knowledge, one should install the *liṅga* within him.
One should cause the life-breaths of the disciple to be deposited within the Śiva-liṅga situated upon the pedestal.
Having established the linga within that vital breath, it then becomes a *prāṇaliṅga*.
Having withdrawn the subtle body (liṅga) into the vital breath (prāṇa), one should practice unification.
O disciple, you should establish the three-fold liṅga; this is your prāṇaliṅga.
Having spoken thus, never at any time separate yourself from the liṅga.
Either on the head, or on the neck, or in the armpit, or even on the chest.
Likewise, the wise man should bear the Prāṇaliṅga upon the surface of his hand as well.
O child, do not abandon this; observe this vow for as long as you live.
Worship the Lord of the gods with supreme personal devotion.
It grants liberation from the bonds of worldly existence, bestows emancipation, and is the cause of all things.
The preceptor should cause [the disciple] to be bathed by officiating priests using water from jars and from sacred fords.
Having lifted them up, one should place the five jars down again and again. || 17 ||
Alternatively, the preceptor himself [represents] the sacred fords situated within the water-pot.
And one should sprinkle the disciple from head to foot with dūrvā sprouts.
In this manner, the preceptor should perform the Aghamarṣaṇa rite three times for him.
At that time, the guru should impart the root mantra to him.
Merely by the sight of the guru, or even by touch or conversation, [the disciple is purified].
The description of the fruit of the Guru’s grace:
one attains the reality of Śiva and shall not undergo rebirth again. || 20 ||
Just as water contained within a pearl oyster certainly becomes a pearl.
Yet it does not again become water, nor does it relinquish its state as a pearl.
Thus he attains the state of Śiva and shall never again return to the state of a bound soul (paśu). || 21 ||

[Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Hand-Worship, the Union of Hands and Head, the Installation of the Six Chakras, Instruction on Mantras, the Wearing of the Linga, the Designated Places, and the Aghamarṣaṇa Bath," in the Section on Initiation within the *Śrīvīraśaivācārapradīpikā*.]
Salutations to the venerable gurus.
[Now begins the ninth chapter:
Next, the sequence for awakening the guru, and the characteristics of the teacher’s fee (guru-dakṣiṇā).
I shall speak; listen properly with diligent attention. (1)
The Guru should teach the Vīramāheśvara Dharma in due order.
In the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava: "Whether walking, standing, sleeping, waking, or even opening and closing the eyes..."
Whether pure or impure, one should wear the liṅga everywhere.
Among all the emblems of Śiva, the Śivaliṅga is praised as the most excellent.
Therefore, that very [object] should indeed be maintained and especially worshipped. || 4 ||
In the navel, the heart, and the head—at all times and in all states.

For that knowledge is indeed one alone, and such is the teaching regarding knowledge.
In the Āditya Purāṇa:
That true reality is the form of the Blessed Lord, the wielder of the trident.
The supreme syllable, the highest ether, the light of Śiva, the Lord of Umā.
In the Yajurveda.

Śiva alone is the one to be worshipped. He, who is the embodiment of the Yajurveda, explains the greatness of the others as being subordinate to Śiva’s status as the object of worship (in the *Caturvedatātparya-saṃgraha*): "The single face..."
The triad of the Lord’s eyes and the four arms—your pure and wondrous body.
For the sake of your ultimate benefit, your divine forms manifest in manifold ways.
Precisely because it is imperishable, they say that the body of the Lord is merely a disguise.
With these firm limbs, your form is imperishable; and those many [limbs] of yours, O bearer of the serpent-garland! (7)

"Those who have praised with firm limbs and bodies" (in another passage), and "The fierce one of many forms with firm limbs"—by such scriptural passages beginning with "unborn," [the Lord] has been shown to possess a form that is not limited by objects; thus it has been stated.
Likewise, in the Yajurveda: "O Rudra, having approached you, some fearful person [says], 'I am unborn... etc.
With that southern face, protect me always; and likewise in the Jābāla Śākhā:
At the end of the age, he stands as the universal remedy; Rudra is indeed alone, for there is no second to stand beside him.
"Neither Brahmā, nor Viṣṇu, nor Sūrya, nor Agni, nor the moon and stars [are its equal]. Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa regarding this matter.
For there are indeed innumerable beings known as Viṣṇus, and innumerable Grandfathers (Brahmās).
The lords of the gods are innumerable, yet Maheśvara alone is eternal.
In the Āditya Purāṇa:
Innumerable are the ages, and indeed innumerable are the grandfathers.
The monkeys are innumerable, yet Maheśvara is eternally one.

You are the destroyer of all, yet there is no destroyer of you; you are the lord of all, yet there is no lord of you.
Having set aside everything else, beginning with Brahmā, you alone—the benefactor of men—are to be meditated upon by people; thus it has been declared.
The Atharvan Veda concludes by stating that liberation is the goal, independent of any other thing to be spoken of.

For this very reason, Sadāśiva—who is not subject to a higher lord, who consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest, whose nature is existence-consciousness-bliss, who bestows auspiciousness, and who is indeed Śiva himself—is the sole granter of liberation. He alone is to be worshipped by those seeking liberation;
he alone is the one object of meditation, having abandoned everything else. (From the Mānava Purāṇa)
Furthermore, by all those seeking liberation, he who is accompanied by Ambā and is called the Lord of All should be worshipped.
By virtue of its specific supreme reality, it should indeed always be meditated upon within the heart.
The deities such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu are to be meditated upon as being subordinate to Him.
Never indeed, out of delusion, should one act with oneself as the primary object. || 13 ||

That [attainment] is likewise divided by the difference in the object of meditation, according to the distinction between superior and inferior.
Among those two types, meditation upon Śiva is the supreme for the gods.
Furthermore, the meditation upon deities such as Viṣṇu and others is considered inferior.
Therefore, by the wise who seek liberation, Śiva alone is the bringer of auspiciousness.
Having abandoned all other deities besides Śiva, he alone should be meditated upon.
O best among those who know the Vedas, in this matter the sacred revelation is perfectly established.
In some instances and at certain times within the Vedas, all other deities besides Him [are mentioned].
